cur:manuscripts-gellone-sacramentary-cru.summary: The opening letter T of the prayer 'Te igitur' at the start of the Canon of the Mass is formed by the cross itself, on which Christ hangs with open eyes and a cross-nimbus, blood streaming from his side, beneath the inscription IHS XPS; two winged angels swoop toward him from above the cross-arm. It is among the earliest images of the Crucifixion placed at the heart of the eucharistic prayer, a practice that became standard in later missals.
facts: Wikipedia describes this page as perhaps the oldest image of the Crucifixion in a Frankish manuscript; the verso of folio 1 shows the Virgin Mary holding a cross and a censer.

The book was at Cambrai Cathedral under Bishop Hildoard (c. 790–800), was later given by William of Gellone to his abbey of Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, passed to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 1638 and entered the French national library in 1796.
cur:manuscripts-gellone-sacramentary-cru.notes: Place of origin is debated (Meaux, Cambrai or another northern French centre).

cur:manuscripts-drogo-crucifixion.summary: Within the round initial O of the Palm Sunday prayers, Christ hangs dead on the cross, his head bowed; a female figure, Ecclesia, holds up a chalice to catch the blood and water from his side, while the Virgin and John stand at either side, a serpent coils at the foot of the cross and the Sun and Moon look on from above. It is one of the earliest images of the suffering, dead Christ (Christus patiens) in Western art.
facts: Wikipedia notes that this Crucifixion is of a new type, the dead 'Christus patiens' rather than the triumphant living Christ that had been the norm.
The motif of Ecclesia catching Christ's blood in a chalice later became entangled with the legend of the Holy Grail.
cur:manuscripts-drogo-crucifixion.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file; the miniature is an initial within the text page.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-adoration-magi.summary: Beneath the star, the three Magi in Phrygian caps approach with gifts, the first kneeling, while the Virgin sits enthroned within a house holding the Christ Child on her lap. The text of the Epiphany Gospel is written above and below the framed image.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.

Egbert gave the book to the church of St Paulin in Trier, where it was used in services until the 18th century; it has been in the Trier city library since 1810 and was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2004 with other Reichenau manuscripts.

cur:objects-cross-of-mathilde-essen.summary: The gilt-bronze body of the crucified Christ hangs at the centre of this jewelled processional cross, his arms outstretched across a field of gold, gems and pearls. On the stem a small enamel shows Abbess Mathilde as donor, kneeling before the Virgin and Child. The crucifix itself contains cavities for relics, making the image of Christ also a reliquary.
facts: Wikipedia notes that it was made between about 1000 and 1058, perhaps in stages, and that the corpus may be a later replacement; the reverse bears a punched Agnus Dei with the evangelist symbols.
It forms a group with the Cross of Otto and Mathilde, the Senkschmelz Cross and the Cross of Theophanu, all made for Essen Abbey.
cur:objects-cross-of-mathilde-essen.notes: Dating straddles the year 1000; included because it was begun under Mathilde (d. 1011).

princeton:33876.summary: On this worn bone plaque Christ, with a large halo, stands at the left and reaches toward the face of a smaller figure beside him, the blind man whose eyes he heals. At the right edge a tall structure with a lattice roof survives from the next scene, the tomb of Lazarus. Plaques like this, pierced for attachment, were probably mounted together to tell the miracles of Christ in sequence.
facts: Princeton records the plaque as possibly Roman or Byzantine, made in Syria or south-eastern Turkey in the 9th–11th century; it measures 9.6 × 8 cm.
It was given in 1994 by Bruce Willsie (Class of 1986) together with the plaque of the Raising of Jairus's daughter (y1994-74), which has consecutive accession numbers.
princeton:33876.notes: Whether the two Willsie plaques come from the same object is not stated by the museum.
